topics.name: Richard Nixon
topics.kicker: 37th U.S. President · The only president to resign
topics.briefing: Richard Nixon grew up in a small California town, made his name as an anti-communist congressman, and became Dwight Eisenhower’s vice president at age 40. As the 37th president, he became the first president to visit Communist China, signed arms-control deals with the Soviet Union, and created the Environmental Protection Agency. The Watergate scandal then made him, in August 1974, the only U.S. president ever to resign.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a member of the House Un-American Activities Committee, this congressman pursued Alger Hiss, a former State Department official whom Whittaker Chambers accused of spying for the Soviet Union. During that case, Chambers led investigators to microfilm hidden inside a hollowed-out pumpkin on his Maryland farm.
tossups.r: This man later served as Dwight Eisenhower’s vice president. For 10 points, name this president who resigned in 1974.

tossups.p: In a 1952 television speech, this candidate answered charges about a fund raised by his supporters and noted that his wife wore a “respectable Republican cloth coat.” He also said his family would keep one gift: a cocker spaniel named Checkers that a supporter in Texas had sent to his young daughters.
tossups.r: He stayed on Dwight Eisenhower’s ticket as the candidate for vice president. For 10 points, name this man who later became the 37th president.

tossups.p: In 1959, this American leader argued with Nikita Khrushchev [“KROOSH-chef”] about capitalism and communism while standing in the kitchen of a model house at an exhibition in Moscow. That exchange became known as the Kitchen Debate.
tossups.r: The next year, he lost a close election to John F. Kennedy. For 10 points, name this vice president who later became the 37th president.

tossups.p: In a bitter 1950 Senate race, this California congressman defeated Helen Gahagan Douglas, a former Broadway actress and opera singer, after his campaign accused her of being soft on communism. Two years earlier, he had made his name in the Alger Hiss case.
tossups.r: He went on to serve eight years as vice president. For 10 points, name this man who resigned the presidency in 1974.

tossups.p: After losing the 1962 race for governor of California to Pat Brown, this man told reporters that they would not have him “to kick around anymore” because this was his “last press conference.” Six years later, he won the presidency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican who defeated Hubert Humphrey in 1968 and later resigned over the Watergate scandal.

tossups.p: In a November 1969 television address, this president asked the “great silent majority” of Americans to support his plan for ending a war in Southeast Asia. Under that plan, American troops came home slowly while South Vietnam’s army took over more of the fighting.
tossups.r: That policy was called Vietnamization. For 10 points, name this president who resigned during the Watergate scandal.

tossups.p: Composer John Adams’s first opera, which premiered in Houston in 1987, opens as this man’s plane lands in a foreign capital and later shows him trading toasts with Premier Zhou Enlai [“JOH en-LYE”] at a banquet. Table tennis matches between American and Chinese players had helped prepare the way for the real trip.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this U.S. president who met Mao Zedong [“MOW dzuh-DONG”] in Beijing in 1972 and later resigned over Watergate.

tossups.p: On August 15, 1971, this president announced that foreign governments could no longer trade U.S. dollars for gold, effectively ending the Bretton Woods system. In the same televised speech, he ordered a 90-day freeze on wages and prices to fight inflation.
tossups.r: His first vice president, Spiro Agnew, resigned in 1973. For 10 points, name this president who resigned in 1974 during the Watergate scandal.

tossups.p: This president signed the National Environmental Policy Act on New Year’s Day 1970 and the Endangered Species Act in 1973. In December 1970, a new federal agency he had proposed began enforcing national rules against air and water pollution.
tossups.r: That agency is the EPA. For 10 points, name this 37th president, who resigned during the Watergate scandal.

tossups.p: At a May 1972 summit in Moscow, this president and Leonid Brezhnev [“BREZH-nef”] signed the SALT I agreement and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, high points of an easing of Cold War tensions called détente [“day-TAHNT”]. His adviser Henry Kissinger helped negotiate those deals.
tossups.r: Months earlier, he had become the first U.S. president to visit Communist China. For 10 points, name this Republican, the 37th president.

tossups.p: In July 1969, this president spoke by radio-telephone from the Oval Office with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin while they stood on the Moon. Days later, he greeted the returning Apollo 11 crew aboard the aircraft carrier _Hornet_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who had lost the 1960 election to John F. Kennedy and resigned in 1974.

tossups.p: This president signed Title IX, a 1972 law that bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money and later helped girls’ sports grow enormously. In 1970, he had signed the law that created OSHA to make workplaces safer.
tossups.r: In 1974, the Supreme Court ordered him to turn over his secret White House tapes. For 10 points, name this president, who resigned over the Watergate scandal about two weeks later.

tossups.p: This man was born in 1913 in a house his father built in Yorba Linda, California, where his presidential library stands. Raised as a Quaker, he graduated from Whittier College and Duke University’s law school, then served in the Navy during World War II.
tossups.r: He won reelection in 1972 over George McGovern. For 10 points, name this Californian, the 37th president.

tossups.p: In 1977 television interviews with British host David Frost, this former president said, “When the president does it, that means that it is not illegal.” Peter Morgan turned those interviews into a play that became a 2008 film starring Frank Langella.
tossups.r: In 1973, he had insisted, “I am not a crook.” For 10 points, name this president who was pardoned by Gerald Ford.

tossups.p: In April 1970, this president announced that American troops were moving into Cambodia to attack enemy bases. Protests broke out on college campuses, and at Kent State University in Ohio, National Guard soldiers shot and killed four students.
tossups.r: The Paris Peace Accords of 1973 ended U.S. combat in Vietnam. For 10 points, name this president, who resigned during the Watergate scandal.

clues.t: 37th President of the United States (1969–1974), a Republican from California
The only U.S. president ever to resign, on August 9, 1974
Resigned because of the Watergate scandal, which began with a break-in at Democratic Party offices in June 1972
First U.S. president to visit Communist China (February 1972), where he met Mao Zedong
Vice President for eight years under Dwight D. Eisenhower (1953–1961)
Lost the close 1960 election to John F. Kennedy after the first televised presidential debates
Won the presidency in 1968 over Hubert Humphrey and George Wallace, then won 49 states against George McGovern in 1972
Vietnamization: brought U.S. troops home slowly while South Vietnam took over the fighting; the Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended U.S. combat
Created the Environmental Protection Agency (1970); signed the Clean Air Act (1970) and the Endangered Species Act (1973)
Détente with the Soviet Union: signed the SALT I arms agreement with Leonid Brezhnev in Moscow (1972)
Vice President Spiro Agnew resigned in 1973; Gerald Ford replaced him, the first vice president chosen under the 25th Amendment
Gerald Ford took over as president and pardoned him in September 1974
In July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled 8–0 that he had to turn over his secret White House tapes
Told reporters in November 1973, “I am not a crook”
As a HUAC congressman, pursued Alger Hiss, accused by Whittaker Chambers of spying for the Soviets; Chambers hid microfilm in a pumpkin (the “Pumpkin Papers”)
“Checkers speech” (1952): on TV he defended a political fund and said his family would keep a gift dog, the cocker spaniel Checkers
Kitchen Debate (1959): argued with Nikita Khrushchev about capitalism and communism in a model American kitchen in Moscow
Won a bitter 1950 Senate race in California over Helen Gahagan Douglas, whom he accused of being soft on communism
After losing the 1962 race for governor of California, told reporters they wouldn’t have him “to kick around anymore”
1969 “Silent Majority” speech asked ordinary Americans who weren’t protesting to support his Vietnam policy
Sent U.S. troops into Cambodia (1970); during the protests that followed, Ohio National Guard soldiers killed four students at Kent State
Ended the dollar’s link to gold (1971), effectively ending the Bretton Woods system, and froze wages and prices for 90 days
Henry Kissinger, his National Security Adviser, secretly visited China in 1971, after “ping-pong diplomacy,” to plan the trip
Subject of composer John Adams’s first opera (1987), about his trip to China
1977 TV interviews with David Frost: “When the president does it, that means that it is not illegal”
Born in Yorba Linda, California (1913); a Quaker who went to Whittier College and Duke’s law school
Spoke by radio-telephone with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon during Apollo 11 (1969)
Signed Title IX (1972), which bans sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money

trap.title: President or scandal?
trap.body: Clues about the tapes, the break-in, and the Saturday Night Massacre show up in two different answer lines: Richard Nixon and the Watergate scandal. If the question asks for “this president,” Watergate is wrong, and if it asks for “this scandal,” Nixon is wrong. Vietnam clues are another trap: Lyndon Johnson sent in huge numbers of troops after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, while Nixon slowly brought them home through “Vietnamization.”
trap.fix: Listen for the noun before you buzz. “This man” or “this president” means Nixon; “this scandal” or “this affair” means Watergate. Gerald Ford is the man who replaced Nixon and pardoned him, so don’t blurt out Ford on a Nixon question.
trap.line: Real answer line: Richard Nixon (or Richard Milhous Nixon)

topics.name: Seneca Falls Convention
topics.kicker: First U.S. women’s rights convention · Launched the fight for the vote
topics.briefing: In July 1848, about 300 people crowded into a small chapel in upstate New York for the first women’s rights convention in the United States. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott led it, and Stanton’s Declaration of Sentiments boldly declared that “all men and women are created equal.” Its demand that women get the right to vote was so controversial that it was the only resolution that did not pass unanimously, but it launched a 72-year fight that ended with the 19th Amendment in 1920.
topics.answerHtml: Seneca Falls Convention (accept Seneca Falls Women’s Rights Convention; prompt on women’s rights convention)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Charlotte Woodward, a young glove maker who signed this event’s most famous document, was the only signer known to have lived to see the 19th Amendment ratified in 1920. That document was signed by 68 women and 32 men.
tossups.r: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized this 1848 meeting. For 10 points, name this first women’s rights convention, held in upstate New York.

tossups.p: James Mott, a Philadelphia merchant, chaired the second day of this event, when the general public was invited to attend. Many of the people at this event were Quakers or abolitionists, and James’s wife was one of its two main organizers.
tossups.r: She was Lucretia Mott, and the other was Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this first U.S. women’s rights convention, held in 1848.

tossups.p: This event was planned over tea at the home of Jane Hunt in Waterloo, New York, by five women, including Mary Ann M’Clintock and Martha Coffin Wright. Wright’s sister, a well-known Quaker minister, helped lead it.
tossups.r: That minister was Lucretia Mott. For 10 points, name this 1848 women’s rights convention, also organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

tossups.p: At this event, the ninth resolution, which said it was the duty of women to secure their “sacred right to the elective franchise,” was the only resolution that did not pass unanimously. Frederick Douglass spoke in favor of that resolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1848 convention in New York that launched the American women’s suffrage movement.

tossups.p: A document read at this event complained that man had made a married woman “civilly dead” in the eye of the law and had taken from her even the wages she earned. Its very first complaint was that women had never been allowed to vote.
tossups.r: That document, the Declaration of Sentiments, was modeled on the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this 1848 women’s rights meeting.

tossups.p: Two of this event’s organizers met in London in 1840, when women who came as delegates to the World Anti-Slavery Convention were made to sit apart and were not allowed to take part. Eight years later, those two women planned this meeting in New York.
tossups.r: They were Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this first women’s rights convention in the United States.

tossups.p: Days after this event, Frederick Douglass praised it in his Rochester newspaper, _The North Star_. At this event, Douglass had argued that women deserved the vote just as much as men, helping one controversial resolution pass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1848 convention led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.

tossups.p: About 300 people, including dozens of men, gathered at the Wesleyan Chapel, a Methodist church that welcomed antislavery speakers, for this two-day event. Most of its organizers were Quakers who were also active in the fight against slavery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first women’s rights convention, organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.

tossups.p: Some of the 100 people who signed this event’s main document later removed their names after newspapers mocked the meeting. Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist editor, was one of the 32 men who signed and kept his name on it.
tossups.r: That document said “all men and women are created equal.” For 10 points, name this 1848 meeting led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

tossups.p: Two weeks after this event, many of its supporters held another women’s rights convention in Rochester, New York, and this time a woman, Abigail Bush, was chosen to preside. This event, by contrast, had been chaired by a man on its second day.
tossups.r: The first one was organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. For 10 points, name this first women’s rights convention in the United States.

tossups.p: In 1980, Congress created the Women’s Rights National Historical Park to preserve the chapel where this event took place, along with the nearby home of one of its organizers. The town where it met is also home to the National Women’s Hall of Fame.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1848 convention led by Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

tossups.p: A Quaker minister who helped lead this event worried that its demand for voting rights would make the meeting look ridiculous, but her co-organizer insisted on including it. That co-organizer wrote most of the event’s main document.
tossups.r: Those women were Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this 1848 women’s rights convention.

tossups.p: Three years after this event, Amelia Bloomer introduced its main organizer to a temperance activist in the same town, beginning a partnership that lasted about 50 years. That newcomer, Susan B. Anthony, had not attended this event.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1848 women’s rights convention in upstate New York, organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

tossups.p: On this event’s 75th anniversary in 1923, Alice Paul announced her proposed Equal Rights Amendment at a gathering in the same town and named it for one of this event’s organizers, a Quaker minister from Philadelphia.
tossups.r: That organizer was Lucretia Mott. For 10 points, name this 1848 meeting where Elizabeth Cady Stanton presented the Declaration of Sentiments.

tossups.p: A newspaper notice announced that this event would discuss “the social, civil, and religious condition and rights of woman” on a Wednesday and Thursday in July. The notice said the first day would be for women only.
tossups.r: Lucretia Mott was among the advertised speakers. For 10 points, name this 1848 meeting in upstate New York, the first women’s rights convention in America.

clues.t: The first women’s rights convention in the United States, held July 19–20, 1848, in upstate New York
Organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott
Stanton’s Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, said “all men and women are created equal”
Its demand for women’s right to vote launched the American women’s suffrage movement
Frederick Douglass spoke up for the voting resolution and helped it pass
Stanton and Mott met in London in 1840, when women were shut out of the World Anti-Slavery Convention
Its Declaration of Sentiments was signed by 100 people: 68 women and 32 men
Held at the Wesleyan Chapel, a Methodist church; about 300 people attended
Susan B. Anthony did not attend; Amelia Bloomer introduced her to Stanton in 1851
The fight it started ended 72 years later with the 19th Amendment (1920)
Lucretia Mott was a Quaker minister and abolitionist; most of the organizers were Quakers
Lucretia Mott’s husband, James Mott, chaired its second day, when the public was invited
Planned over tea at Jane Hunt’s home in Waterloo, New York, by five women, including Mary Ann M’Clintock and Martha Coffin Wright
The ninth resolution, on the “elective franchise” (the vote), was the only one that did not pass unanimously
Even Lucretia Mott worried that demanding the vote would make the meeting look ridiculous
Charlotte Woodward, a young glove maker, was the only signer known to have lived to see the 19th Amendment ratified
Its declaration said men had made married women “civilly dead” under the law and had taken even the wages they earned
Frederick Douglass praised the meeting in his Rochester newspaper, _The North Star_
A follow-up women’s rights convention met in Rochester two weeks later, with Abigail Bush presiding
A newspaper notice called it a meeting about “the social, civil, and religious condition and rights of woman”; the first day was for women only
The Women’s Rights National Historical Park (1980) preserves the chapel; the town also has the National Women’s Hall of Fame
Some signers later removed their names after newspapers mocked the meeting
Alice Paul announced the Equal Rights Amendment at its 75th anniversary celebration (1923) and named it for Lucretia Mott

trap.title: Where was Susan B. Anthony?
trap.body: Susan B. Anthony is the most famous suffragist, so players often assume she was at Seneca Falls, but she did not attend; she met Elizabeth Cady Stanton three years later, in 1851. Players also mix up this 1848 meeting with its own document, the Declaration of Sentiments, and with later meetings such as Worcester (1850), the first national women’s rights convention, and Akron (1851), where Sojourner Truth spoke.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this meeting” or “this convention,” say Seneca Falls; if it asks for “this document,” say the Declaration of Sentiments. Seneca Falls clues: 1848, Stanton and Lucretia Mott, the Wesleyan Chapel, 68 women and 32 men, and Frederick Douglass.
trap.line: Real answer line: Seneca Falls Convention (prompt on women’s rights convention)

topics.name: Spanish-American War
topics.kicker: 1898 war between the U.S. and Spain · Made America an overseas power
topics.briefing: In February 1898, the American warship _Maine_ exploded in the harbor of Havana, Cuba, and many newspapers blamed Spain. About two months later, the United States was at war, winning at sea in the Philippines and on land in Cuba, where Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders charged up Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill. The war lasted less than four months, and in the peace treaty Spain gave the United States Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
topics.answerHtml: Spanish-American War (or War of 1898; accept Spanish–Cuban–American War; prompt on Cuban War of Independence)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A 1976 investigation led by Admiral Hyman Rickover concluded that a fire in a coal bunker, not a mine, most likely caused the explosion that helped start this war. A U.S. Navy court of inquiry at the time had instead blamed a mine for that blast.
tossups.r: That blast sank the USS _Maine_, inspiring the slogan “Remember the _Maine_!” For 10 points, name this 1898 war between the United States and Spain.

tossups.p: William Randolph Hearst’s _New York Journal_ published a stolen private letter in which the diplomat Enrique Dupuy de Lôme called President William McKinley weak. Days later, an explosion destroyed an American warship, pushing the nation closer to this war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which the United States fought Spain over Cuba.

tossups.p: To crush a rebellion, General Valeriano Weyler forced hundreds of thousands of rural people into crowded “reconcentration” camps, and American newspapers nicknamed him “the Butcher.” Reports about those camps helped build American support for this war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war that ended Spanish rule in Cuba and Puerto Rico.

tossups.p: The poet José Martí [“mar-TEE”] was killed in 1895, soon after returning home to lead a revolt that eventually led to this war. That revolt’s fighters, led by generals such as Máximo Gómez, battled for their island’s independence for three years before the United States joined in.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which the United States fought Spain over Cuba.

tossups.p: Elbert Hubbard’s 1899 essay “A Message to Garcia” praised Lieutenant Andrew Rowan, who carried a message from the U.S. government to a rebel general at the start of this war. Hubbard used Rowan’s journey to celebrate people who get a job done without asking a lot of questions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war that began soon after the sinking of the USS _Maine_ in Havana Harbor.

tossups.p: “You may fire when you are ready, Gridley,” said the commodore aboard the cruiser _Olympia_ during this war’s first major battle. His squadron slipped past island forts in the dark and then destroyed an enemy fleet without losing a single American ship.
tossups.r: That battle, won by George Dewey on May 1, 1898, took place at Manila Bay in the Philippines. For 10 points, name this 1898 war fought against Spain.

tossups.p: Richmond Hobson tried to trap an enemy fleet during this war by sinking the coal ship _Merrimac_ in the narrow entrance to Santiago Harbor. When Admiral Pascual Cervera’s ships finally tried to escape that harbor on July 3, American warships destroyed them.
tossups.r: John Hay, soon to be Secretary of State, called this conflict “a splendid little war.” For 10 points, name this 1898 war against Spain.

tossups.p: The 9th and 10th Cavalry, Black regiments nicknamed Buffalo Soldiers, helped capture Kettle Hill outside Santiago during this war. On that same day, other American troops attacked the nearby town of El Caney.
tossups.r: Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders also charged up Kettle Hill and nearby San Juan Hill on July 1, 1898. For 10 points, name this 1898 war against Spain.

tossups.p: According to a famous but doubtful story, William Randolph Hearst told the artist Frederic Remington, “You furnish the pictures and I’ll furnish the war,” after Remington reported that all was quiet. Hearst’s _New York Journal_ battled Joseph Pulitzer’s _New York World_ for readers.
tossups.r: Their sensational “yellow journalism” helped stir up this war. For 10 points, name this 1898 conflict fought mainly over Cuba.

tossups.p: Senator Henry Teller of Colorado added an amendment promising that the United States would not annex one island after this war. A later amendment named for Orville Platt let the U.S. step in on that island and lease a naval base at Guantánamo [“gwahn-TAH-nuh-moh”] Bay.
tossups.r: That island was Cuba. For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which the United States defeated Spain.

tossups.p: Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie joined the Anti-Imperialist League to oppose taking over the Philippines after this war. In 1899, the Senate barely approved the treaty that ended this war.
tossups.r: In that Treaty of Paris, Spain gave the United States Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. For 10 points, name this 1898 war.

tossups.p: Rudyard Kipling’s 1899 poem “The White Man’s Burden” urged Americans to take control of lands won in this war. The Filipino leader Emilio Aguinaldo [“ah-ghee-NAHL-doh”], who had fought against his islands’ old colonial rulers during this war, then led Filipino forces against the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war after which the U.S. paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines.

tossups.p: Far more American soldiers died of diseases such as typhoid and yellow fever than in combat during this war, and some troops complained about spoiled canned “embalmed beef.” Afterward, Walter Reed’s team confirmed that mosquitoes spread yellow fever.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which Theodore Roosevelt led the Rough Riders.

tossups.p: Writers known as the Generation of ’98, such as Miguel de Unamuno [“oo-nah-MOO-noh”], reflected on their country’s crushing defeat in this war, which Spaniards called “the Disaster.” That defeat ended their country’s empire in the Americas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States.

tossups.p: When the cruiser _Charleston_ fired at an old fort on Guam during this war, officials on the island thought it was a salute because they had not heard that the war had begun. A few weeks later, the United States annexed Hawaii through the Newlands Resolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 war in which the United States also won the Philippines and Puerto Rico.

clues.t: Fought in 1898 between the United States and Spain; it lasted less than four months
Sparked by the explosion of the USS _Maine_ in Havana Harbor, Cuba (February 15, 1898): “Remember the _Maine_!”
Fought mainly over Cuba, where rebels had been fighting for independence since 1895
Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders charged up Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill near Santiago, Cuba (July 1, 1898)
Treaty of Paris (1898): Spain gave up Cuba and gave the U.S. Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines (for $20 million)
“Yellow journalism” in William Randolph Hearst’s _New York Journal_ and Joseph Pulitzer’s _New York World_ stirred up war fever
Commodore George Dewey destroyed Spain’s Pacific fleet at Manila Bay in the Philippines (May 1, 1898)
President William McKinley asked Congress to declare war in April 1898
Diplomat John Hay, soon to be Secretary of State, called it “a splendid little war”
The Teller Amendment (1898) promised that the U.S. would not annex Cuba
The Platt Amendment (1901) let the U.S. intervene in Cuba and lease a naval base at Guantánamo Bay
Far more U.S. soldiers died of diseases like typhoid and yellow fever than in battle
The Anti-Imperialist League, including Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie, opposed taking over the Philippines
General Valeriano Weyler (“the Butcher”) forced rural Cubans into crowded “reconcentration” camps
The de Lôme letter (February 1898): a Spanish diplomat privately called McKinley weak, and Hearst’s paper printed it
Hearst supposedly told artist Frederic Remington, “You furnish the pictures and I’ll furnish the war”
A 1976 study by Admiral Hyman Rickover found that a coal-bunker fire, not a mine, most likely sank the _Maine_
At Manila Bay, Dewey told the captain of his flagship _Olympia_, “You may fire when you are ready, Gridley”
U.S. warships destroyed Admiral Pascual Cervera’s fleet as it fled Santiago Harbor (July 3, 1898); Richmond Hobson had tried to trap it by sinking the _Merrimac_
The 9th and 10th Cavalry, Black regiments called Buffalo Soldiers, fought at Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill
Filipino leader Emilio Aguinaldo fought Spain, then fought the U.S. in the Philippine-American War (1899–1902)
Rudyard Kipling’s 1899 poem “The White Man’s Burden” urged the U.S. to rule the Philippines
Elbert Hubbard’s essay “A Message to Garcia” (1899) praised Andrew Rowan for carrying a message to a Cuban rebel general
Spaniards called the defeat “the Disaster”; writers such as Miguel de Unamuno became known as the Generation of ’98
Poet José Martí, a hero of Cuban independence, was killed in 1895, soon after the revolt against Spain began
Afterward, Walter Reed’s team in Cuba confirmed that mosquitoes spread yellow fever (1900)
The cruiser _Charleston_ took Guam, where officials hadn’t heard that war had begun; the U.S. also annexed Hawaii (Newlands Resolution, July 1898)

trap.title: Not Mexico, not the Philippines
trap.body: Three American wars sound alike. The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) won California and the Southwest, the Spanish-American War (1898) ended Spanish rule in Cuba, and the Philippine-American War (1899–1902) began when Filipinos led by Emilio Aguinaldo fought U.S. rule. The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) was a different war, fought among Spaniards inside Spain.
trap.fix: Listen for 1898, Cuba, the _Maine_, Manila Bay, San Juan Hill, the Rough Riders, and yellow journalism. Zachary Taylor, Santa Anna, and the Mexican Cession mean the Mexican-American War; Aguinaldo fighting U.S. troops after 1899 means the Philippine-American War.
trap.line: Real answer line: Spanish-American War (or War of 1898; accept Spanish–Cuban–American War; prompt on Cuban War of Independence)

topics.name: Susan B. Anthony
topics.kicker: Leader of the fight for women’s suffrage · Arrested for voting in 1872
topics.briefing: In November 1872, Susan B. Anthony walked into a polling place in Rochester, New York, and cast a ballot for president, even though women were not allowed to vote. She was arrested, put on trial, and fined $100, which she refused to pay. With her partner Elizabeth Cady Stanton, she fought for women’s right to vote for more than 50 years, and the 19th Amendment that finally won it in 1920 was nicknamed for her.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young teacher, this woman learned that men were paid far more than women for the same work, and in the 1840s she headed the girls’ department at Canajoharie [“kan-uh-juh-HAIR-ee”] Academy in New York. Raised as a Quaker, she later left teaching to work full-time for reform causes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested for voting in 1872 and later appeared on a dollar coin.

tossups.p: In 1852, men at a Sons of Temperance meeting in Albany would not let women speak, so this woman and her closest ally started a women’s temperance society. She later worked as a New York agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society.
tossups.r: That ally was Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this suffragist who was arrested for voting in Rochester in 1872.

tossups.p: During the Civil War, this woman and a close friend founded the Women’s Loyal National League, which gathered about 400,000 signatures on petitions asking Congress to end slavery with a constitutional amendment. That amendment became the 13th Amendment in 1865.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reformer who was fined $100 after voting in the 1872 presidential election.

tossups.p: In 1868, this woman began publishing a weekly newspaper called _The Revolution_, paid for at first by the businessman George Francis Train, with her longtime partner as its editor. The paper ran up large debts, which this woman spent years paying off.
tossups.r: That partner was Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this suffragist who was honored on a dollar coin in 1979.

tossups.p: Her longtime partner described their teamwork by saying, “I forged the thunderbolts, she fired them,” because this woman delivered many of the speeches her partner wrote. This woman never married and spent decades traveling to give lectures.
tossups.r: Her partner was Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this leader of the women’s suffrage movement.

tossups.p: At a June 1873 trial in Canandaigua [“kan-un-DAY-gwuh”], New York, Judge Ward Hunt did not let this defendant testify and ordered the jury to find her guilty. She told the judge she would never pay a dollar of his “unjust penalty.”
tossups.r: She had been arrested for voting in the 1872 election. For 10 points, name this suffragist.

tossups.p: Before her trial, this woman toured her home county giving a speech titled “Is It a Crime for a Citizen of the United States to Vote?” In it, she argued that the Constitution’s “we, the people” meant “the whole people,” women as well as men.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested for voting in Rochester in 1872.

tossups.p: This woman worked with Matilda Joslyn Gage and her best-known partner to write the first volumes of the _History of Woman Suffrage_, which began appearing in 1881. In 1869, she and that same partner had founded the National Woman Suffrage Association.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this suffragist whose face appeared on a dollar coin first minted in 1979.

tossups.p: This woman was born in 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts, to a Quaker family that opposed slavery and believed in educating girls. Her family later moved to a farm near Rochester, New York, the city that became her home.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested in Rochester for voting in 1872 and became the most famous leader of the fight for women’s suffrage.

tossups.p: In 1851, Amelia Bloomer introduced this woman on a street to the main organizer of a famous convention held in the same New York town three years earlier. This woman had not attended that 1848 convention.
tossups.r: Her new friend was Elizabeth Cady Stanton. For 10 points, name this suffragist, who was arrested for voting in 1872.

tossups.p: In 1869, this woman co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association after she opposed the 15th Amendment for leaving out women. Lucy Stone and others formed a rival group, the American Woman Suffrage Association, and the two groups did not merge until 1890.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this suffragist who worked for decades with Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

tossups.p: From 1892 to 1900, this woman served as president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, and then she handed that job to Carrie Chapman Catt. She had taken over the group from her longtime friend, its first president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this suffragist who died 14 years before the 19th Amendment was ratified.

tossups.p: At her 86th birthday celebration in Washington in February 1906, this woman ended her last public speech with the words “Failure is impossible.” She died about a month later at her home in Rochester, New York.
tossups.r: The 19th Amendment was later nicknamed for her. For 10 points, name this suffragist.

tossups.p: In 1878, California senator Aaron Sargent, at the urging of this woman and her partner, introduced a constitutional amendment saying that the right to vote could not be denied “on account of sex.” It took more than 40 years for Congress to pass it.
tossups.r: Ratified in 1920 as the 19th Amendment, it was nicknamed for her. For 10 points, name this suffragist.

tossups.p: On Election Day, many voters in Rochester, New York, place “I Voted” stickers on this woman’s gravestone in Mount Hope Cemetery. Her house in that city, where she died in 1906, is a museum.
tossups.r: A dollar coin honoring her was first minted in 1979. For 10 points, name this suffragist who was arrested for voting in 1872.

clues.t: Leader of the 1800s fight for women’s suffrage (the right to vote)
Arrested for voting in the 1872 presidential election in Rochester, New York
Worked side by side with Elizabeth Cady Stanton for about 50 years
Honored on a dollar coin first minted in 1979, the first circulating U.S. coin to show a real woman
The 19th Amendment (1920) was nicknamed for her; she died 14 years before it was ratified
At her 1873 trial, Judge Ward Hunt ordered the jury to find her guilty; she never paid her $100 fine
Ended her last public speech, at her 86th birthday celebration in 1906, with “Failure is impossible”
Co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association with Stanton in 1869
Opposed the 15th Amendment because it left out women, splitting the movement from Lucy Stone’s rival group
President of NAWSA (1892–1900), formed when the rival groups merged in 1890; Carrie Chapman Catt followed her
Began in the temperance movement; when men wouldn’t let her speak at an 1852 meeting, she and Stanton started a women’s temperance society
Worked as a New York agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society
Was not at the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention; Amelia Bloomer introduced her to Stanton in 1851
A teacher in her youth, she saw that women teachers were paid far less than men; in the 1840s she headed the girls’ department at Canajoharie Academy
During the Civil War, her Women’s Loyal National League gathered about 400,000 signatures for an amendment to end slavery
Published the newspaper _The Revolution_ (starting in 1868), first funded by George Francis Train, with Stanton as editor
Stanton said of their teamwork: “I forged the thunderbolts, she fired them”
Her trial was held in Canandaigua, New York, and the judge did not let her testify
Before her trial, gave the speech “Is It a Crime for a Citizen of the United States to Vote?” arguing that “we, the people” meant “the whole people”
Co-wrote the _History of Woman Suffrage_ (from 1881) with Stanton and Matilda Joslyn Gage
Born in 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts, and raised as a Quaker
Senator Aaron Sargent introduced her “on account of sex” amendment in 1878; the same words became the 19th Amendment
On Election Day, voters put “I Voted” stickers on her grave in Rochester’s Mount Hope Cemetery

trap.title: Anthony or Stanton?
trap.body: Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton worked side by side for about 50 years, so their clues often appear in the same tossups. Stanton organized the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention and wrote the Declaration of Sentiments, but Anthony was not there; she met Stanton in 1851. Players also mix Anthony up with Lucy Stone, who led a rival suffrage group starting in 1869, and with Alice Paul, who led protests in the 1910s.
trap.fix: Anthony clues: voting in Rochester in 1872, her trial and unpaid $100 fine, “Failure is impossible,” the 1979 dollar coin, and the amendment nicknamed for her. Stanton clues: Seneca Falls, the Declaration of Sentiments, seven children, and _The Woman’s Bible_.
trap.line: Real answer line: Susan B. Anthony (or Susan Brownell Anthony)

topics.name: Ulysses S. Grant
topics.kicker: Union general who won the Civil War · 18th U.S. President
topics.briefing: Ulysses S. Grant failed as a farmer and businessman before the Civil War, but once the fighting began he won a string of key victories in the West, including the capture of Vicksburg. Abraham Lincoln put him in charge of all Union armies, and in April 1865 Robert E. Lee surrendered to him at Appomattox Court House. Grant then served two terms as the 18th president, and while dying of cancer he wrote memoirs that became a best seller.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man was born Hiram in Point Pleasant, Ohio, in 1822, but Congressman Thomas Hamer wrote down the wrong name when nominating him to West Point, giving him a new middle initial. His classmates there nicknamed him “Sam.”
tossups.r: He later fought in the Mexican-American War. For 10 points, name this Union general who accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender and became the 18th president.

tossups.p: In the 1850s, this man built a log house he called “Hardscrabble” on a farm near St. Louis and sold firewood on the city’s streets. When a war began in 1861, he was working as a clerk in his family’s leather goods store in Galena, Illinois.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who rose to command all Union armies in the Civil War.

tossups.p: In his memoirs, this general called the Mexican-American War, in which he had fought as a young officer, one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger nation against a weaker one. In that war, he served as his regiment’s quartermaster, keeping its soldiers supplied.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who later served two terms as president, from 1869 to 1877.

tossups.p: In February 1862, this general told his old friend Simon Bolivar Buckner that “no terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender” would be accepted at Fort Donelson in Tennessee. Days earlier, this general had captured nearby Fort Henry.
tossups.r: Newspapers joked that his initials stood for “Unconditional Surrender.” For 10 points, name this Union general and later president.

tossups.p: In April 1862, Albert Sidney Johnston’s Confederates surprised this general’s army near Pittsburg Landing, Tennessee, but Johnston was killed, and reinforcements under Don Carlos Buell helped this general win on the second day. That battle was named for a small log church.
tossups.r: That battle was Shiloh. For 10 points, name this Union general who later captured Vicksburg.

tossups.p: Benjamin Grierson’s cavalry raid through Mississippi distracted Confederate defenders while this general marched his army south and crossed the Mississippi River below his target in 1863. After a siege of more than six weeks, John C. Pemberton surrendered that city to him.
tossups.r: That city was Vicksburg, which fell on July 4, 1863. For 10 points, name this Union general.

tossups.p: In November 1863, this general broke the siege of Chattanooga, Tennessee, after Union troops won the Battle of Lookout Mountain and then charged up Missionary Ridge. A few months later, Congress revived the rank of lieutenant general so that he could be promoted.
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln then put him in charge of all Union armies. For 10 points, name this general who later became the 18th president.

tossups.p: During fighting at Spotsylvania Court House in May 1864, this general wrote, “I propose to fight it out on this line if it takes all summer.” His Overland Campaign also included the Battle of the Wilderness and a failed assault at Cold Harbor.
tossups.r: That campaign wore down Lee’s army in Virginia. For 10 points, name this Union general who became the 18th president.

tossups.p: Ely Parker, a Seneca officer on this general’s staff, wrote out the final copy of the surrender terms that this general offered in Wilmer McLean’s parlor in April 1865. Those generous terms let Confederate soldiers go home and take their own horses with them.
tossups.r: Robert E. Lee surrendered to him at Appomattox Court House. For 10 points, name this Union general.

tossups.p: In January 1868, this general angered President Andrew Johnson by giving up his job as acting Secretary of War so that Edwin Stanton could return to the office. Months later, the Republicans nominated this general for president, and he ran with the slogan “Let us have peace.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who won the 1868 election and became the 18th president.

tossups.p: On September 24, 1869, a day called Black Friday, gold prices crashed after this president ordered the Treasury to sell gold, ruining a plan by Jay Gould and James Fisk to corner the market. This president’s brother-in-law, Abel Corbin, had been part of their scheme.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 18th president, whose two terms also saw the Whiskey Ring scandal.

tossups.p: Under this president, Secretary of State Hamilton Fish negotiated the Treaty of Washington with Britain in 1871. An international panel in Geneva then ordered Britain to pay $15.5 million for damage done by the _Alabama_ and other British-built Confederate raiders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president from 1869 to 1877, who had earlier commanded the Union armies.

tossups.p: In 1871, this president used new Enforcement Acts to send troops and federal prosecutors against the Ku Klux Klan, even suspending habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”] in nine South Carolina counties. The Department of Justice, created in 1870 during his first term, led many of those prosecutions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 18th president, who had commanded the Union armies at the end of the Civil War.

tossups.p: In 1872, this president signed the law creating Yellowstone, the world’s first national park. That same year, he won reelection over Horace Greeley, a newspaper editor who died before the Electoral College voted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 18th president, who had led the Union armies to victory in the Civil War.

tossups.p: While dying of throat cancer at Mount McGregor, New York, this man raced to finish his memoirs, which Mark Twain’s publishing company sold with huge success to support his family. He and his wife, Julia, lie in Manhattan’s Riverside Park, in the largest mausoleum in North America.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Civil War general and 18th president, whose face is on the $50 bill.

clues.t: Commanding general of all Union armies, who led the North to victory in the Civil War
Accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865
18th President of the United States (1869–1877), a Republican
His face is on the fifty-dollar ($50) bill
Captured Vicksburg, Mississippi, after a siege (July 4, 1863), giving the Union control of the Mississippi River
Demanded “unconditional and immediate surrender” from Simon Bolivar Buckner at Fort Donelson (1862); people joked his initials meant “Unconditional Surrender”
Survived a surprise attack at Shiloh, Tennessee (April 1862), and won on the second day
Graduated from West Point (1843) and fought in the Mexican-American War
As president, enforced Reconstruction and used troops and federal courts against the Ku Klux Klan (1871)
Scandals during his presidency included the Whiskey Ring and Crédit Mobilier
Wrote his _Personal Memoirs_ while dying of throat cancer; Mark Twain’s company published them (1885)
Signed the 1872 law creating Yellowstone, the first national park
Promoted to lieutenant general in 1864 and given command of all Union armies
Fought Lee in the 1864 Overland Campaign (the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor), then besieged Petersburg
Born Hiram (1822, Point Pleasant, Ohio); Congressman Thomas Hamer’s mistake on his West Point nomination changed his name
In the 1850s, farmed at “Hardscrabble” near St. Louis; in 1861 he was clerking in the family leather store in Galena, Illinois
His memoirs called the Mexican-American War one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger nation against a weaker one
At Spotsylvania (1864): “I propose to fight it out on this line if it takes all summer”
Ely Parker, a Seneca on his staff, wrote out the surrender terms; Parker later became the first Native American Commissioner of Indian Affairs
Lee surrendered in Wilmer McLean’s parlor; the terms let Confederate soldiers go home with their own horses
Broke the siege of Chattanooga (November 1863) with wins at Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge
As acting Secretary of War, he angered Andrew Johnson by giving the office back to Edwin Stanton (1868)
Won in 1868 with the slogan “Let us have peace”; in 1872 he beat Horace Greeley, who died before the electoral vote
Black Friday (1869): Jay Gould and James Fisk tried to corner the gold market until his Treasury sold gold
The Department of Justice was created in 1870, during his first term; he suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties to fight the Klan
Secretary of State Hamilton Fish’s Treaty of Washington (1871) settled the Alabama Claims; Britain paid $15.5 million
Buried in New York City’s Riverside Park, in the largest mausoleum in North America

trap.title: Which Union general?
trap.body: Tossups about this man are crowded with other Civil War names. Robert E. Lee surrendered to him at Appomattox, William Tecumseh Sherman was his most trusted general and marched through Georgia, George McClellan led the Union army early in the war, and George Meade won at Gettysburg. Blurting out a name you just heard in the question is the fastest way to lose this tossup.
trap.fix: Grant clues: Fort Donelson’s “unconditional surrender,” Shiloh, Vicksburg, Appomattox, the 18th presidency, and memoirs published by Mark Twain. Plain “Grant” is enough, but “Ulysses” alone is not.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ulysses S. Grant (or Hiram Ulysses Grant)

topics.name: Watergate scandal
topics.kicker: 1970s political scandal · Led to Richard Nixon’s resignation in 1974
topics.briefing: On June 17, 1972, a security guard noticed tape holding door latches open in a Washington, D.C., office building, and police caught five burglars inside the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters. Reporters, a Senate committee, and secret White House tape recordings slowly revealed that President Richard Nixon and his aides had tried to cover up links to the crime. Facing likely impeachment, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the early morning hours, security guard Frank Wills noticed that someone had taped door latches open in a Washington office building, removed the tape, and then found the doors taped again on his next round. That building complex stands next to the Kennedy Center on the Potomac River.
tossups.r: Police then caught five burglars in the Democratic National Committee’s offices. For 10 points, name this scandal that led Richard Nixon to resign.

tossups.p: In July 1973, former White House aide Alexander Butterfield surprised a Senate committee by revealing that a secret system had been recording conversations in the Oval Office. Investigators then spent a year fighting to get those recordings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal, whose tapes eventually forced President Richard Nixon to resign.

tossups.p: In October 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy, William Ruckelshaus [“RUCK-ulz-howss”], resigned rather than obey an order to fire special prosecutor Archibald Cox. Solicitor General Robert Bork then carried out the firing.
tossups.r: That night became known as the Saturday Night Massacre. For 10 points, name this scandal that ended Richard Nixon’s presidency.

tossups.p: In 2005, Mark Felt, who had been the FBI’s second-ranking official during this scandal, revealed that he was the secret source who had met a reporter late at night in a parking garage to share information about it.
tossups.r: That source, nicknamed “Deep Throat,” helped Bob Woodward of the _Washington Post_. For 10 points, name this scandal that began with a 1972 break-in.

tossups.p: An 18½-minute gap was found on one recording in this scandal, and the president’s secretary, Rose Mary Woods, said she might have erased part of it by accident while transcribing. She showed reporters an awkward stretch she said she had made while answering the phone.
tossups.r: That tape belonged to President Richard Nixon. For 10 points, name this scandal that led to his resignation.

tossups.p: Senator Howard Baker of Tennessee famously asked, “What did the President know, and when did he know it?” during this scandal’s televised hearings. Those 1973 hearings were led by Senator Sam Ervin of North Carolina.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal that began with a break-in at Democratic Party offices in 1972.

tossups.p: White House counsel John Dean warned his boss that there was “a cancer” close to the presidency, and he later told Senate investigators about efforts to hide the truth in this scandal. Dean had been fired in April 1973.
tossups.r: In November 1973, Richard Nixon insisted, “I am not a crook.” For 10 points, name this scandal involving a cover-up by Nixon’s aides.

tossups.p: A recording from June 23, 1972, released in August 1974, showed the president approving a plan to have the CIA ask the FBI to slow down its investigation in this scandal. That “smoking gun” evidence cost the president most of his remaining support in Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal that led Richard Nixon to resign just days after that tape was released.

tossups.p: In a unanimous 1974 decision written by Chief Justice Warren Burger, the Supreme Court ruled that executive privilege did not let the president keep evidence in this scandal secret. Special prosecutor Leon Jaworski [“juh-WOR-skee”] had asked the court to order the release of that evidence.
tossups.r: That case, _United States v. Nixon_, forced the release of White House tapes. For 10 points, name this scandal.

tossups.p: G. Gordon Liddy and E. Howard Hunt, who helped plan this scandal’s central crime, had earlier worked for the “Plumbers,” a White House unit formed to stop leaks. In 1971, the Plumbers broke into the office of Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist after Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this political scandal that began with a 1972 break-in and led to Richard Nixon’s resignation.

tossups.p: Judge John Sirica, nicknamed “Maximum John” for his tough sentences, received a letter from defendant James McCord in March 1973 saying that the burglars had been pressured to stay silent. That letter helped break open this scandal.
tossups.r: Gerald Ford said “our long national nightmare is over” when it ended. For 10 points, name this scandal that forced Richard Nixon to resign in August 1974.

tossups.p: Texas congresswoman Barbara Jordan declared that her “faith in the Constitution is whole” as the House Judiciary Committee, chaired by Peter Rodino, debated articles of impeachment during this scandal in July 1974. The committee approved three articles.
tossups.r: Those articles accused President Richard Nixon of obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress. For 10 points, name this scandal.

tossups.p: In a 1976 film based on a book about this scandal, Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman played two reporters, and a secret source tells one of them to “follow the money.” Jason Robards won an Oscar for playing their editor, Ben Bradlee.
tossups.r: That film was _All the President’s Men_. For 10 points, name this scandal uncovered by _Washington Post_ reporters.

tossups.p: Former Attorney General John Mitchell, who had led a campaign committee that critics nicknamed “CREEP,” went to prison for his role in this scandal. Top White House aides H. R. Haldeman and John Ehrlichman [“ER-lik-mun”] resigned in April 1973 and were later convicted too.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal that led President Richard Nixon to resign in 1974.

tossups.p: After this scandal, Congress created the Federal Election Commission to enforce campaign finance rules and later passed the Ethics in Government Act of 1978. The second half of this scandal’s name became a suffix used to name many later scandals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal that began with a 1972 break-in at a Washington, D.C., office complex.

clues.t: Led President Richard Nixon to resign on August 9, 1974, the only presidential resignation in U.S. history
Began with a June 17, 1972, break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s offices in a Washington, D.C., building complex
Nixon and his aides tried to cover up the White House’s links to the burglars, including paying them hush money
Secret recordings of Oval Office conversations, the White House tapes, proved the cover-up
_Washington Post_ reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein uncovered much of the story
Their secret source, “Deep Throat,” turned out to be FBI official Mark Felt (revealed in 2005)
Their book _All the President’s Men_ (1974) became a 1976 film starring Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman
_United States v. Nixon_ (July 1974): the Supreme Court ruled 8–0 that Nixon had to hand over the tapes
“Saturday Night Massacre” (October 1973): special prosecutor Archibald Cox was fired after Elliot Richardson and William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than fire him
The burglars were linked to the Committee to Re-elect the President, nicknamed “CREEP,” led by John Mitchell
A Senate committee led by Sam Ervin held televised hearings in 1973
In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment against Nixon
Gerald Ford became president (“Our long national nightmare is over”) and pardoned Nixon in September 1974
Nixon told reporters in November 1973, “I am not a crook”
Security guard Frank Wills found tape holding door latches open and called the police
Former White House aide Alexander Butterfield revealed the secret White House taping system to the Senate in July 1973
White House counsel John Dean warned Nixon of “a cancer” close to the presidency, then testified against him
Senator Howard Baker asked, “What did the President know, and when did he know it?”
An 18½-minute gap on one tape; secretary Rose Mary Woods said she might have erased part of it by accident
The “smoking gun” tape (June 23, 1972) showed Nixon approving a plan to have the CIA slow the FBI’s investigation
Planners G. Gordon Liddy and E. Howard Hunt had worked for the “Plumbers,” who broke into the office of Pentagon Papers leaker Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist
Judge John Sirica (“Maximum John”) got a 1973 letter from burglar James McCord saying the defendants had been pressured to stay silent
Leon Jaworski replaced Cox as special prosecutor; Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the tapes decision
Texas congresswoman Barbara Jordan said her “faith in the Constitution is whole”; Peter Rodino chaired the House Judiciary Committee
Top aides H. R. Haldeman and John Ehrlichman resigned in April 1973 and were later convicted, as was John Mitchell
Led to the Federal Election Commission and the Ethics in Government Act (1978), and gave later scandals the suffix “-gate”
The office and hotel complex stands beside the Potomac River, next to the Kennedy Center

trap.title: Scandal, not president
trap.body: Tossups about this scandal are packed with clues about Richard Nixon, but answering “Nixon” when the question asks for “this scandal” is wrong. Players also confuse it with other scandals: Teapot Dome (secret oil leases under Warren Harding in the 1920s), the Pentagon Papers (a secret history of the Vietnam War leaked in 1971), and Iran-Contra (secret arms sales under Ronald Reagan in the 1980s).
trap.fix: “This scandal” or “this affair” wants Watergate; “this president” wants Nixon. A 1972 break-in, burglars, Deep Throat, the Saturday Night Massacre, or an 18½-minute gap all point to Watergate.
trap.line: Real answer line: Watergate scandal (or Watergate affair; accept Watergate break-in)

topics.name: Battle of Antietam
topics.kicker: Bloodiest single day in U.S. history · Led to the Emancipation Proclamation
topics.briefing: On September 17, 1862, Union and Confederate armies fought along Antietam Creek in western Maryland, and by nightfall about 23,000 soldiers had been killed, wounded, or gone missing. It is still the bloodiest single day in American history. Robert E. Lee’s first invasion of the North ended, and five days later Abraham Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Antietam (or Battle of Sharpsburg; prompt on Maryland Campaign)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Days before this battle, Corporal Barton Mitchell of the 27th Indiana found a copy of Special Order 191 wrapped around three cigars in a field near Frederick. That “Lost Order” revealed that Robert E. Lee had divided his army.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this September 1862 battle in Maryland, the bloodiest single day in American history.

tossups.p: Two days before this battle, Stonewall Jackson captured about 12,000 Union soldiers at Harpers Ferry, the largest surrender of U.S. troops during the Civil War. Jackson then hurried most of his men north to rejoin Robert E. Lee’s army.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of September 17, 1862, which led to the Emancipation Proclamation.

tossups.p: Three days before this battle, Union troops pushed through Turner’s, Fox’s, and Crampton’s Gaps in the Battle of South Mountain. Robert E. Lee then pulled his army back behind a nearby creek, where this battle began at dawn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1862 battle, the bloodiest single day in American history.

tossups.p: At dawn during this battle, Joseph Hooker’s corps attacked south through a farmer’s cornfield toward the Dunker Church, and John Bell Hood’s Texans launched a fierce counterattack. That field changed hands again and again during the morning.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this September 1862 battle in Maryland between George McClellan and Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: During this battle, John Sedgwick’s Union division suffered heavy losses in the West Woods near the Dunker Church, a small white meetinghouse of German Baptist Brethren. Photographs taken near that church after the fighting became some of the war’s best-known images.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that ended Robert E. Lee’s first invasion of the North in 1862.

tossups.p: Thomas Meagher’s [“MAR”] Irish Brigade charged toward Confederates defending a sunken farm road during this battle, and that road was later nicknamed “Bloody Lane.” The Confederates there finally fell back after one of their officers misunderstood an order.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this one-day battle fought in Maryland on September 17, 1862.

tossups.p: A few hundred Georgians under Robert Toombs held off Union attackers for hours at a stone bridge during this battle. The Union general whose troops finally captured that bridge gave it his name.
tossups.r: That general was Ambrose Burnside. For 10 points, name this battle where George McClellan fought Robert E. Lee in 1862.

tossups.p: Late in the afternoon of this battle, A. P. Hill’s division arrived after a hard march of about 17 miles from Harpers Ferry and struck the Union flank, saving Robert E. Lee’s army from defeat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle along a Maryland creek, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War.

tossups.p: During this battle, the Union commander kept thousands of soldiers in reserve, including Fitz John Porter’s corps, instead of sending them into the fight. Afterward, he let the enemy army retreat across the Potomac River into Virginia without chasing it.
tossups.r: That commander, George McClellan, was removed weeks later. For 10 points, name this September 1862 battle.

tossups.p: Clara Barton brought a wagon of medical supplies onto this battlefield and cared for wounded soldiers close to the fighting, and a surgeon there called her the “Angel of the Battlefield.” She later founded the American Red Cross.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1862 battle that gave Abraham Lincoln the victory he needed to announce the Emancipation Proclamation.

tossups.p: Future president William McKinley, then a young commissary sergeant in an Ohio regiment, brought hot coffee and food to soldiers under fire during this battle, and a monument on the battlefield honors him. Another future president, Rutherford B. Hayes, had been wounded leading that regiment three days earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of September 17, 1862, the bloodiest day in American history.

tossups.p: Alexander Gardner photographed soldiers who had died on this battlefield, and Mathew Brady displayed the pictures in his New York gallery that October. A newspaper wrote that Brady had brought home the “terrible reality” of war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1862 battle where George McClellan faced Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: In October 1862, Abraham Lincoln visited the army camped near this battlefield, and Alexander Gardner photographed him meeting the army’s commander inside a tent. Frustrated that the commander would not chase the enemy, Lincoln removed him from command a month later.
tossups.r: That general was George McClellan. For 10 points, name this battle fought in Maryland in September 1862.

tossups.p: Britain and France had been considering whether to step in and help negotiate an end to the Civil War, but this battle’s outcome convinced them to wait. Neither country ever recognized the Confederacy.
tossups.r: Five days after this battle, Abraham Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation. For 10 points, name this 1862 battle in Maryland.

tossups.p: Robert E. Lee’s army slipped away from this battlefield at night and crossed the Potomac River at Boteler’s Ford near Shepherdstown. Union troops who followed were pushed back in a small fight there.
tossups.r: That retreat ended Lee’s first invasion of the North. For 10 points, name this bloodiest one-day battle in American history.

clues.t: The bloodiest single day in American history: about 23,000 soldiers killed, wounded, or missing
Fought on September 17, 1862, along a creek in western Maryland
Treated as a Union victory, it let Abraham Lincoln announce the Emancipation Proclamation five days later (September 22, 1862)
Union general George McClellan fought Confederate general Robert E. Lee
Ended Lee’s first invasion of the North, the Maryland Campaign
Union soldiers found a copy of Lee’s battle plans, Special Order 191 (the “Lost Order”), wrapped around three cigars
Morning: the armies fought back and forth through the Cornfield
Midday: Confederates defended the Sunken Road, later nicknamed “Bloody Lane”
Afternoon: Ambrose Burnside’s troops spent hours trying to cross a stone bridge, later called Burnside’s Bridge
A tactical draw, but Lee retreated across the Potomac River into Virginia
McClellan didn’t chase Lee, so Lincoln removed him from command in November 1862
The result discouraged Britain and France from recognizing the Confederacy
Confederates named it after the nearby Maryland town; the Union usually named battles after creeks and rivers
Two days before, Stonewall Jackson captured about 12,000 Union troops at Harpers Ferry, the largest U.S. surrender of the war
A. P. Hill’s division arrived from Harpers Ferry late in the day and saved Lee’s right flank
Three days earlier, Union troops pushed through the gaps of South Mountain (September 14, 1862)
Fighting swirled around the Dunker Church, a small white church, and the nearby West Woods
Joseph Hooker’s corps opened the battle at dawn; John Bell Hood’s Texans counterattacked in the Cornfield
Thomas Meagher’s Irish Brigade charged the Sunken Road
A few hundred Georgians under Robert Toombs held the stone bridge for hours
McClellan held back thousands of reserve troops, including Fitz John Porter’s corps
Clara Barton brought supplies and nursed the wounded; she was called the “Angel of the Battlefield”
Alexander Gardner’s photographs of the battlefield, shown at Mathew Brady’s New York gallery, showed Americans the war’s human cost
Lincoln visited McClellan near the battlefield in October 1862; Gardner photographed them in a tent
Future president William McKinley, a commissary sergeant, brought coffee and food to Ohio soldiers under fire

trap.title: Antietam or Gettysburg?
trap.body: Both battles ended a Confederate invasion of the North led by Robert E. Lee, and both had enormous losses, so players mix them up. Antietam (September 1862, Maryland) was the bloodiest single day, ended Lee’s first invasion, and led to the Emancipation Proclamation. Gettysburg (July 1863, Pennsylvania) lasted three days, ended Lee’s second invasion, and led to the Gettysburg Address.
trap.fix: McClellan, the Lost Order, the Cornfield, Bloody Lane, Burnside’s Bridge, and September 1862 mean Antietam. “Sharpsburg” is also correct, because Confederates often named battles after nearby towns.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Antietam (or Battle of Sharpsburg; prompt on Maryland Campaign)

topics.name: Battle of Yorktown
topics.kicker: Cornwallis’s 1781 surrender · Effectively ended the American Revolution
topics.briefing: In August 1781, British general Lord Cornwallis dug in at Yorktown, a tobacco port on Virginia’s York River, expecting help from the Royal Navy. Instead, a French fleet blocked the Chesapeake Bay, while George Washington’s Americans and the Comte de Rochambeau’s French soldiers surrounded the town and pounded it with cannons. On October 19, Cornwallis surrendered his whole army, which effectively ended the American Revolution.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Yorktown (or Siege of Yorktown; prompt on descriptions of Cornwallis’s surrender)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Claiming to be ill, the losing commander at this battle sent his deputy, Charles O’Hara, to the surrender ceremony, where O’Hara tried to hand his sword to the Comte de Rochambeau [“roh-sham-BOH”]. Rochambeau pointed him toward the American commander, who sent him to his own second-in-command, Benjamin Lincoln.
tossups.r: Lord Cornwallis had surrendered his army. For 10 points, name this 1781 battle in Virginia that effectively ended the American Revolution.

tossups.p: John Trumbull’s painting of the surrender that ended this battle hangs in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda. It shows Benjamin Lincoln riding a white horse between a line of French officers and a line of American officers.
tossups.r: That painting is titled _Surrender of Lord Cornwallis_. For 10 points, name this 1781 battle in Virginia.

tossups.p: James Armistead, an enslaved man, posed as a runaway to spy on the British camp before this battle, and he later took the last name of the French general he worked for, the Marquis de Lafayette. Virginia’s legislature freed him in 1787.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1781 siege where Lord Cornwallis surrendered to George Washington.

tossups.p: One night near the end of this siege, the trapped commander tried to ferry his troops across a river to Gloucester Point, but a sudden storm scattered his boats. The next morning, he asked for terms.
tossups.r: That commander was Lord Cornwallis. For 10 points, name this battle on Virginia’s York River that effectively ended the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Officers from both sides met at the Augustine Moore House on October 18 to work out the Articles of Capitulation that ended this siege. John Laurens helped negotiate them for the Americans, and they were signed the next day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1781 siege where Lord Cornwallis surrendered his army to American and French forces.

tossups.p: The Comte de Barras [“bah-RAHS”] sailed from Newport, Rhode Island, carrying the heavy French siege guns used in this battle. Those cannons and American guns began bombarding the enemy’s defenses on October 9.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau trapped Lord Cornwallis.

tossups.p: When Lord George Germain brought him news of this battle, Prime Minister Lord North reportedly cried out, “Oh God! It is all over!” North resigned a few months later, in March 1782.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1781 battle in Virginia, where the surrender of Lord Cornwallis’s army effectively ended the American Revolution.

tossups.p: At the end of this siege, the defeated army was denied the honors of war and had to march out with its flags cased, as revenge for the way Americans who surrendered at Charleston in 1780 had been treated.
tossups.r: According to legend, a band played “The World Turned Upside Down” during the surrender. For 10 points, name this 1781 battle in Virginia where Lord Cornwallis surrendered.

tossups.p: After winning a costly victory over Nathanael Greene at Guilford Courthouse in North Carolina, the British commander at this battle marched north into Virginia, where the Marquis de Lafayette’s small army shadowed him. That commander then fortified a tobacco port to wait for British ships.
tossups.r: That commander was Lord Cornwallis. For 10 points, name this 1781 siege where he surrendered.

tossups.p: During this siege, Henry Knox commanded the American artillery, and soldiers dug long trenches called parallels so they could move their cannons closer to the enemy’s earthworks. The first parallel was begun on October 6.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in Virginia where Lord Cornwallis surrendered to George Washington.

tossups.p: On October 17, exactly four years after John Burgoyne’s surrender at Saratoga, a British drummer and an officer waving a white handkerchief appeared on the defenses during this battle to ask for a cease-fire.
tossups.r: Two days later, Lord Cornwallis’s army surrendered. For 10 points, name this battle that effectively ended the American Revolution.

tossups.p: On the night of October 14, French troops captured Redoubt No. 9 during this siege, while Americans led by Alexander Hamilton stormed Redoubt No. 10 with bayonets. Capturing those two small forts let the attackers extend their trench lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1781 siege in Virginia where Lord Cornwallis surrendered to George Washington.

tossups.p: On September 5, a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse [“GRAHSS”] drove off British ships under Thomas Graves in the Battle of the Chesapeake, cutting off any rescue by sea for the British army at this battle.
tossups.r: De Grasse had sailed north from the Caribbean with thousands of French soldiers. For 10 points, name this 1781 siege where George Washington trapped Lord Cornwallis.

tossups.p: Weeks before this battle, American and French armies secretly marched south from New York, fooling the British commander Henry Clinton into expecting an attack on New York City. A national historic trail follows their route to this battle.
tossups.r: Those armies were led by George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau. For 10 points, name this battle where Lord Cornwallis surrendered.

tossups.p: A few months before this siege, Anthony Wayne’s Americans narrowly escaped a trap set by the British army at the Battle of Green Spring, near Jamestown. The town where this siege took place forms Virginia’s Historic Triangle with Jamestown and Williamsburg.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1781 battle where Lord Cornwallis surrendered, effectively ending the American Revolution.

trap.title: Yorktown or Saratoga?
trap.body: Two big Revolutionary War surrenders get mixed up. At Saratoga (1777, New York), John Burgoyne surrendered to Horatio Gates, and that victory convinced France to join the war; at Yorktown (1781, Virginia), Charles Cornwallis surrendered to Washington and the French, which effectively ended the war. Players also blurt out the Battle of the Chesapeake, the French naval victory that trapped Cornwallis, or Jamestown, Yorktown’s neighbor in Virginia’s Historic Triangle.
trap.fix: Burgoyne, Gates, Benedict Arnold, and 1777 mean Saratoga; Cornwallis, Rochambeau, de Grasse, Redoubt No. 10, and 1781 mean Yorktown. If the question asks for “this naval battle,” the answer is the Battle of the Chesapeake (also called the Battle of the Virginia Capes).
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Yorktown (or Siege of Yorktown; prompt on descriptions of Cornwallis’s surrender)
